name: Uma Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for talking to me, Uma. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group. We're not connected to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties. This is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Can you describe a normal day at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the card services line for a high-street bank. People ring when they've lost their card, when a payment's been blocked, or when they think someone's stolen their money. I follow the script on the screen, check who they are, freeze the card, order a new one. I've been there a year and a half and I still get flustered with the fraud ones.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what's difficult?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that there's a right way to do things. The script tells you, and if you follow it you're safe. What's hard is when someone's crying because their rent's gone from their account, and I have to stay calm and read the next line. My manager says I stick to the script too much and need to think on my feet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's okay by me. I'd be happy if it just stayed like this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say well, there you go, people still want a person when their money goes missing. At work I'd probably just say it to the girls at my bank of desks. I don't post anything online, I only read.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still be a bit worried, because the bank keeps pushing everyone onto the app. Calls are already down since they put the freeze-your-card button in there. Even a little bit of automation takes the easy calls, and the easy calls are the ones I'm good at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and keep doing the job. I'd try to get better at the fraud calls by asking the senior lady on my team to let me listen in. I'd keep putting a bit aside each month, I've got about two months saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, if I'm honest. Things are changing even when they say nothing's changing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the easy calls are the ones you're good at. Can you say more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The lost card calls are simple, I can do those in my sleep. The fraud ones need you to make decisions, and I hate that. If the bank's app takes all the simple calls, I'm left with the calls I'm worst at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does Jonas, your boyfriend, worry about any of this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. He drives a delivery van, he says nobody's going to replace him anytime soon. He thinks I worry too much, and maybe I do.

say: I'd say people still want a **real person** when their money goes missing.
I'd only say it at my desk, because I **never post** online.
think: The bank's **app** already takes the simple calls away.
The **easy calls** are the ones I handle best.
do: Keep doing the job and **listen in** on a senior colleague's fraud calls.
Keep saving a little each month towards **two months** already saved.
feel: **Uneasy**, sensing change even when told nothing is changing.
S0.quote: If the bank's app takes all the simple calls, I'm left with the calls I'm worst at.
fieldNote: She sees that even small automation **strips the easy calls** she depends on.
She finds safety in **the script** and dreads having to decide things.
Her boyfriend's **van job** feels secure to both of them.

steps.text: Listen in on a senior colleague's fraud calls to learn them
Keep adding a little each month to her two months of savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds like it's about my job, really. Answering customers is right there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's sad, but that's business, banks will always look for the cheaper way. I'd say people should still be able to talk to a human about their money. I'd probably tell my mum that I'm fine, so she doesn't worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm one of the ones who goes. I don't use any of the AI things and I'm not quick on the fraud calls. When the team shrinks, they'll keep the experienced ones who can think on their feet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop buying clothes and eating lunch out, and try to get my savings up to four months. I'd look at jobs that aren't on a phone, maybe at the big supermarket or in a pharmacy, because those are near my flat. And I'd talk to my parents about moving back if it came to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, to be honest. It feels like the ground's going soft under me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why not learn the AI tools to stay on the team?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've tried looking at them. Learning the AI tools feels like learning a whole new language when I'm still learning the old one. My brain just doesn't take to it. I'd rather do something I understand, even if it pays less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Jonas the night they announced cuts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him I need to find something else, and he'd say don't panic. Then I'd lie awake doing sums on my phone calculator. His wage alone could cover the rent, just about, but not much else.

say: I'd say it's sad, but **that's business**, and banks chase the cheaper way.
I'd tell my mum **I'm fine** so she doesn't worry.
think: I'm likely **one of the ones** who goes when the team shrinks.
They'll keep agents who **think on their feet**, and I don't.
do: Stop clothes shopping and lunches out to reach **four months** of savings.
Apply for **supermarket or pharmacy** jobs near her flat.
Ask her parents whether she could **move back**.
feel: **Frightened**, as if the ground is going soft under her.
S1.quote: Learning the AI tools feels like learning a whole new language when I'm still learning the old one.
fieldNote: She expects to be **cut** and doesn't fight it, just plans around it.
She'd rather take a **lower-paid** familiar job than learn AI tools.
Her **centre** outlook shows: no blame, just 'that's business'.

steps.text: Stop buying clothes and lunches out until savings reach four months
Apply for supermarket or pharmacy jobs near her flat
Ask her parents if she could move back home for a while

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years? I wouldn't even know where to start with that one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say somebody in charge should have seen this coming. I'd probably just repeat what everyone else is saying. I wouldn't have anything clever to add.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd lose my job inside two years and so would everyone on my floor. And my boyfriend Jonas, his van could be driven by a robot three years after that. So it's not just me, it's both of us, and I have no idea what either of us would do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I honestly don't know. I'd cut everything but rent and food, and I'd probably wait for the government to say something, because I wouldn't know which way to jump. We were going to look at getting a place together with a garden next year, and I'd put that off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panicked. I can feel my chest going tight just saying it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't know which way to jump. If you had to pick one thing, what would it be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe cleaning, or care work, something with my hands. But I don't know anyone who does those, and I'd be starting from nothing. In two years I wouldn't even be trained before everyone else was trying the same thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing at first, because Mum worries. Then probably that we might need to come and stay for a bit. They've got a spare room, but it's full of Dad's fishing stuff.

say: I'd say someone in charge **should have seen** this coming.
I'd just **repeat** what everyone else was saying.
think: I'd lose my job within **two years**, along with my whole floor.
My boyfriend's **van job** could go to robots soon after.
do: Cut spending to **rent and food** only.
**Wait for the government** to say something before choosing a direction.
Put off **moving in** together to a place with a garden.
S2.quote: I'd lose my job inside two years and so would everyone on my floor. And my boyfriend Jonas, his van could be driven by a robot three years after that.
fieldNote: Two years leaves her with **no plan** and no idea where to start.
She sees both **household incomes** at risk, not just her own.
She'd **wait for the government** because she can't pick a direction.

steps.text: Cut spending to rent and food only
Wait for a government plan before choosing a new job
Put off renting a place with a garden with Jonas
Ask her parents to clear the spare room in case

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's a bit better. At least you could get ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time, so the banks and the government should help people move into other work. I'd say it calmly, because five years sounds like a long time when you say it out loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still be gone by about 2031. But I'd have time to learn something hands-on. Robots don't come until around 2034, so if I learned hairdressing or care work I'd have a few more years after the call centre goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do a hairdressing course at the college, the evening one. I used to cut my friends' hair at school and I liked it. I'd keep working at the bank and keep saving until I had a few months more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, still, but it feels like I could do something with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you avoid new things. How would starting a course feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scary, but hairdressing isn't really new to me. Hairdressing is scissors and a comb, not a computer. I'd be more nervous about walking into the college than about the cutting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Jonas think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd be pleased, I think. He's always said I'm good with people when I'm not reading off a screen.

say: I'd say banks and government should help people **move into other work**.
I'd say it **calmly**, since five years sounds long.
think: I'd still lose the bank job by about **2031**.
Hairdressing or care would give me **extra years** before robots.
do: Enrol in an **evening hairdressing** course at the college.
Keep working at the bank and **keep saving** a few more months.
feel: **Worried**, but she feels she could **do something** with five years.
S3.quote: Hairdressing isn't really new to me. Hairdressing is scissors and a comb, not a computer.
fieldNote: Five years lets her pick a **familiar, hands-on** skill rather than freeze.
She still expects to **lose the job**, so the worry stays high.
Her plan comes from an **old hobby**, not from research.

steps.text: Enrol in the college's evening hairdressing course
Keep the bank job and save a few more months

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. That feels a long way off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time, so let's not get carried away. I'd say the same thing to my mum. Nobody really knows what will happen in ten years anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd probably keep doing what I'm doing for a good few years, because I like routine. I'd think about the hairdressing again maybe halfway through. The bank job would go eventually, but not next week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job and keep saving. Maybe in three or four years I'd do the hairdressing course, if things looked like they were really coming. I'd want to see the bank actually cutting people before I did anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer. I could put it out of my mind most days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you wait until you see cuts, is that too late?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. But I've seen people panic about things before that never happened. I'd rather not throw away a decent job for something that might not come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you start earlier?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the bank let go of the senior lady on my team, the best one we have, I'd know it was real. She trained half of us.

say: I'd say ten years is **plenty of time** and not to get carried away.
I'd say **nobody knows** what will happen in ten years.
think: I'd keep my **routine** for a good few years.
The bank job would go **eventually**, but not next week.
do: Keep her bank job and **keep saving** each month.
Consider the **hairdressing course** in three or four years.
Wait to see **real cuts** before acting.
feel: **Calmer**, able to put it out of her mind most days.
S4.quote: If the bank let go of the senior lady on my team, the best one we have, I'd know it was real.
fieldNote: A decade lets her **fall back on routine** and delay.
Her signal is a **trusted colleague** being cut, not news or data.
She still expects to **lose the job** in time, so anxiety stays under the calm.

steps.text: Keep working the card services line and saving monthly
Wait to see whether the bank cuts senior staff before acting
Sign up for hairdressing in three or four years if cuts begin

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it takes my job and then Jonas's, and I'd have no idea what to do. What would help is someone telling me clearly which jobs will still be there, and a course I could do without having to be good with computers.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about people who aren't good with technology. Everyone talks like we'll all just learn new things. Some of us aren't built that way, and we still need to pay rent.

headlineQuote: Everyone talks like we'll all just learn new things. Some of us aren't built that way, and we still need to pay rent.
portrait: Uma is 27 and works the **card services line** at a high-street bank.
She feels safe following **the script** and struggles with fraud calls that need judgement.
She **never uses AI** and would rather take a familiar lower-paid job.
Her boyfriend drives a **delivery van**, so the fast scenario threatens both incomes.
Her fallback idea is **hairdressing**, a skill she already enjoyed at school.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because it would take her job and then her boyfriend's.
whatWouldHelp: Clear advice on **which jobs** will still exist.
A **course** that doesn't require being good with computers.
